notes.1: Most candidates were able to give the correct answer. There were some answers of obtuse and some not related to angles.
notes.2: Although most candidates gave the correct answer, a small number gave 5.6 or 5600.
notes.3: Most candidates gave the correct answer. The most common incorrect answer was 4300.
notes.4: Many candidates understood how to factorise. A small number tried to combine the terms to give 17x or 27x or made an equation to reach a numerical answer. Some tried to take x out as a factor in addition to 3.
notes.5a: This question was almost always correctly answered. There were a few blank responses and (6 – 2 × 5) was seen a number of times.
notes.5b: This part was also very well answered with the most common incorrect answer being (8 + 6). Some candidates put in more than one pair of brackets.
notes.6a: The majority of candidates answered correctly but 10 and 4 were seen at times.
notes.6b: This part was almost always correctly answered. �PAGE�10
notes.7a: Almost all candidates knew cube numbers and answered this part correctly. Common incorrect answers were 47 and 87.
notes.7b: There were many correct answers in this part. Common incorrect answers were 57 and 87. A small number of candidates wrote the same number for both parts or more than one number.
notes.8a: This part was generally well answered. Some of the incorrect responses were due to not knowing 5 5 where was on the scale, rather than not knowing that the probability is . A small number gave 8 8 the three-quarter mark and some drew arrows between the given marks on the scale.
notes.8b: This part was very well answered although was seen (probability of red).
notes.9: Finding just the reduction, 100.8, was the main error. The vast majority of candidates answered correctly. Almost all did this question in stages and it was very rare to see 560 × 0.82.
notes.10: Candidates confused area and circumference and also radius and diameter. A few used an inaccurate value of π, 3.14. The most common error was to find the area of the circle. There were also quite a few candidates giving their final answer as 9 (the diameter).
notes.11: There were a significant number of candidates who did not know what was meant by standard form. Some just rewrote 72000 and 0.0018 in the answer space. Others rounded the given numbers to one significant figure.
notes.11a: Those who knew standard form almost always got the answer correct. 72 × 103 and 720 × 102 were the most common incorrect answers.
notes.11b: This was not so well answered with an index of 3 instead of –3 being a common error.
notes.12: This question was well attempted. Most expansions were correct but the middle terms were occasionally missing. Also seen were correct expansions but incorrect combining terms or other errors in the final answer. Some gave 2x instead of x2 for the first term. Candidates should ensure they write their final answer on the answer line.
notes.13a: Many correct answers were seen in this part. The main incorrect answers were x9, or 18 from multiplying the indices.
notes.13b: Almost all answers were correct for this part although 10 from 2 + 10 = 12 was seen occasionally.
notes.14: Many candidates knew to use Pythagoras’ theorem. This was a ‘show that’ question but many did not understand that they needed to give an answer more accurate than 41.8 to gain full credit. Several attempted trigonometry but did not give a full method. Several candidates did not make any attempt at this question. �PAGE�11
notes.15a: This question was almost always correctly answered.
notes.15b: Most answers were correct for the mode. The most common incorrect answers were 7 or both 7 and grey on the answer line.
notes.16: Although volume was found a significant number of times, many candidates were able to give the correct answer. Many gained partial credit for just one area or repeating areas more than twice.
notes.17: The majority of candidates were able to give the correct answer to all three parts. The main errors were with the addition or subtraction of negative numbers. Only a small number incorrectly wrote a fraction line in the vector.
notes.18: Many candidates scored full marks for a correct list. Some just multiplied each number by 30. Quite a few candidates, after dividing by 12, rounded before multiplying by 30.
notes.19: There were many correct answers seen to this problem solving question, although quite a number did not take an algebraic approach to find the correct value of n. Some made progress with the algebra but there were errors in the manipulation.
notes.20a: The majority of candidates were able to give the correct co-ordinates.
notes.20b: Plotting the point was well done but a few plotted at other points on the line y = 3.
notes.20c: Most candidates knew rhombus. Parallelogram was seen a few times and kite sometimes after a correct (1, 3) for point D.
notes.20d: Several candidates did not understand rotational symmetry with 4 being a common incorrect answer.
notes.21a: This part was almost always correctly answered. The most common incorrect answer was 45.
notes.21b: This part was not as well answered. Many candidates either stated that the graph needed extending or ignored the fact that the graph does not show $420 and just described how to read off a graph, e.g. find 420 on the x-axis then read up to the line and across. For those who had the right idea there was a variety of correct methods, common ones included $42 × 10, $21 × 20 or $35 × 12. Some chose values too low on the line, usually suggesting reading $1 which was not accurate enough.
notes.21c: Most candidates produced accurate lines, although some did not attempt the part. Incorrect lines were usually due to values being used that were too low for accuracy. �PAGE�12
notes.22a: Almost all candidates read the value correctly although a few misread the scale.
notes.22b: The points were generally plotted correctly.
notes.22c: The majority of candidates were able to draw a ruled line of best fit within tolerance. A small number joined all the points.
notes.22d: Although many candidates were able to state negative, several gave a description. Direct was seen several times.
notes.23a: Several candidates scored full credit for a correct bisector with correct arcs. Others scored partial credit for a bisector without arcs. Some had bisected the incorrect angle.
notes.23b: Most candidates understood that an arc was needed and many correct ones were seen. This was the most successful part of this question.
notes.23c: Candidates found this part very challenging and it was rare to award credit. �PAGE�13
notes.key_messages:
To succeed in this paper candidates need to have completed full syllabus coverage, remember necessary
formulae and definitions and show all working clearly. Ensure that the questions are read carefully.
notes.general_comments:
The vast majority of candidates were able to attempt all the questions in the time given. Working was
generally well presented with clear writing. Some candidates prematurely rounded in the middle of a
question. Candidates should be encouraged to show the method, even though they are using a calculator.
